findings.who: A filer moved into a newly built home in early 2025. The builder had finished installing rooftop solar panels and a 10 kWh battery in late 2024.
findings.why_no: The help says 'It counts for 2025 if the installation was finished in 2025.' Here the installation was finished in 2024. The filer also did not 'have anything installed'; the builder put it in before they owned the home.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 1, Costs: 'For purposes of the residential clean energy credit only, costs connected with the construction of a home are treated as being paid when your original use of the constructed home begins'; p. 1, Caution: 'The residential clean energy credit (Part I) is available for both existing homes and homes being constructed.'
findings.fix: Add to the gate: 'or did you start living in a newly built or rebuilt home in 2025 that came with any of these?' Amend the help: 'For a newly built or rebuilt home, it counts for the year you first moved in, not the year the installation was finished.'

findings.who: A filer's fire-damaged home was rebuilt. New windows, insulation and a heat pump were installed in December 2024, and the filer moved back in during February 2025.
findings.why_no: The help ties the year to when the installation was finished, which was 2024. The filer therefore answers no for 2025.
findings.line: f5695.windows_if_any, f5695.insulation_if_any, f5695.heat_pump_if_any (and other Part II lines)
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 1, Costs: 'For purposes of both credits, costs are treated as being paid when the original installation of the item is completed, or, in the case of costs connected with the reconstruction of your home, when your original use of the reconstructed home begins.'
findings.fix: Amend the help: 'If your home was rebuilt, it counts for the year you began living in the rebuilt home.'

findings.who: A condominium owner, or a co-op tenant-stockholder, whose association installed solar panels, a central boiler, or new windows on the building in 2025. The work was paid from association funds or a special assessment.
findings.why_no: They did not 'have anything installed at home' themselves. The association did the work, and the cost reached them as a fee or assessment, not as their own purchase.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 2, Association or cooperative costs: 'If you are a member of a condominium management association for a condominium you own or a tenant-stockholder in a cooperative housing corporation, you are treated as having paid your proportionate share of any costs of such association or corporation.'
findings.fix: Add to the gate: 'Include work your condo association or housing co-op had done on your building, even if you paid for it only through fees or an assessment.'

findings.who: A filer installed solar panels or a geothermal heat pump at a vacation cabin or second home in 2025. Alternatively, they installed a ground-mounted array, a wind turbine, or a battery elsewhere on their property rather than on the house.
findings.why_no: 'At home' reads as the main home, or as on or in the house itself. A second residence, or equipment out on the land, does not seem to count.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 2: 'The home doesn't have to be your main home'; 'installed on or in connection with your home located in the United States'; p. 2, Residential Clean Energy Credit (Part I): 'If you made energy saving improvements to more than one home that you used as a residence during 2025...'
findings.fix: Ask 'at any home you lived in during 2025, including a second or vacation home, or on its property.'

findings.who: A filer bought insulation, air-sealing materials, or an exterior door in 2025 and installed it themselves.
findings.why_no: 'Did you have anything installed' suggests hiring an installer. A do-it-yourself project may not seem to count.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 3, Section A: 'Any insulation material or system and air sealing material or system that is specifically and primarily designed to reduce heat loss or gain of a home when installed in or on such a home'; 'don't include amounts paid for the onsite preparation, assembly, or original installation of the building envelope component.'
findings.fix: Reword as 'did you install, or have someone install, ...'.

findings.who: A filer paid a certified auditor for a home energy audit in 2025 but installed nothing.
findings.why_no: The question asks only about things 'installed'. Only the help adds that an audit counts, and a filer who does not read the help answers no.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 2, Energy Efficient Home Improvement Credit (Part II): '3. The amount paid or incurred for home energy audits during 2025'; p. 3: 'A credit limit of $150 for home energy audits.'
findings.fix: Put the audit in the question itself: '...or pay for a home energy audit?'

findings.who: A filer replaced branch circuits or feeders, but not the panel itself, to serve a new heat pump or heat pump water heater.
findings.why_no: The help names only an 'electrical panel'. New circuits or feeders do not seem to be something that 'saves or makes energy'.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 3, Section B: 'Certain improvements or replacements of panelboards, subpanelboards, branch circuits, or feeders.'
findings.fix: Amend the help: 'An electrical panel, subpanel, or new circuits or feeders put in for such equipment count too.'

findings.who: A condominium owner or co-op tenant-stockholder whose condominium association or cooperative housing corporation paid a certified auditor in 2025 to inspect the building and write a report. The filer's share of that cost came through assessments or maintenance charges, not an invoice to them.
findings.why_no: "A home energy audit was paid for" reads as an audit the filer bought and paid for. The association hired the auditor, and the filer never saw a bill, so they answer no.
findings.line: f5695.line26a_if_audit (and with it the line 26b amount and the line 26c credit of up to $150)
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 2, Association or cooperative costs: "you are treated as having paid your proportionate share of any costs of such association or corporation"; p. 2: "3. The amount paid or incurred for home energy audits during 2025"
findings.fix: Ask: "In 2025, did you or your spouse pay for a home energy audit (also called an energy assessment or evaluation) of a home you lived in? Include an audit paid for by your condominium association or housing cooperative, even if your share came through dues or assessments."

findings.who: A homeowner who paid a utility-affiliated program or contractor in 2025 for a "home energy assessment" or "energy evaluation" (for example, a blower-door test and inspection) and got a written report from a certified auditor.
findings.why_no: Nothing they paid for was called an "audit". They read "home energy audit" as a specific product they never bought, and answer no.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 3, Home energy audits: "Home energy audit costs are costs for an inspection and written report for your main home located in the United States that: 1. Identifies the most significant and cost-effective energy efficiency improvements"
findings.fix: Describe the thing, not only its name: "an inspection of your home by an energy auditor or assessor, with a written report recommending energy improvements (often called a home energy audit, assessment, or evaluation)." Let line 26a then test whether the auditor was certified.

findings.who: A filer whose audit was performed in 2025 and billed in 2025, but whose payment cleared in early 2026, or who financed the audit fee.
findings.why_no: "Was paid for in 2025" reads as payment made in 2025. The instructions' general rule counts amounts "paid or incurred" during 2025.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 2: "You may be able to take a credit equal to 30% of the sum of: ... 3. The amount paid or incurred for home energy audits during 2025"
findings.fix: Ask "paid for or performed in 2025", and let the line 26b amount question apply the paid-in-2025 rule from the line instructions.

findings.who: A homeowner whose contractor did a certified energy audit with a written report as part of a 2025 insulation or heat pump job, with the audit priced inside the overall contract.
findings.why_no: They paid for the installation, not separately for an audit, so they answer no to "a home energy audit was paid for".
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 7, Line 26b: "Enter the amounts you paid for home energy audits in 2025."
findings.fix: In the help, add: "Include an audit done by your installer, even if it was part of a larger contract, if you received a separate written audit report."

findings.who: A filer who had a wood-pellet or wood-burning stove, a fireplace insert, or a wood/pellet hydronic boiler installed in 2025. The manufacturer certifies it at 75% thermal efficiency (HHV) and gives a QMID.
findings.why_no: The filer knows it as a 'pellet stove', 'wood stove' or 'insert', not a 'biomass stove or biomass boiler', and answers no to the unfamiliar term.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 7: 'Line 29e. Enter the QMID and amount you paid for the most expensive biomass stove or biomass boiler that has a thermal efficiency rating of at least 75%'
findings.fix: Ask: 'Was a stove, fireplace insert, furnace or boiler that burns wood, wood pellets, corn or other plant material installed in 2025 at a home you or your spouse used (including a building whose condo association or co-op you belong to)?' Then classify by efficiency rating and QMID.

findings.who: A filer who installed a wood or pellet stove in 2025 as the home's heat source, replacing an old stove or oil heat.
findings.why_no: The parent gate asks whether anything was installed 'to save or make energy'. The filer sees a heater that burns fuel and does neither, so answers no, and the biomass question is never reached.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 3, Section B: 'Qualified energy property is any of the following. ... Certain biomass stoves and biomass boilers.'
findings.fix: In the parent gate, list the heating and cooling equipment explicitly: 'any furnace, boiler, stove (including wood or pellet), heat pump, water heater, central air conditioner, electrical panel, insulation, windows, doors, solar or battery'. Do not rely on the phrase 'save or make energy'.

findings.who: Married filers on a joint return who lived apart in separate main homes in 2025. The spouse had a qualifying pellet boiler installed at the spouse's home.
findings.why_no: Neither the parent nor the child gate says 'you or your spouse'. The filer answers for the household's own home, where nothing was installed.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 3, Married taxpayers with more than one home: 'If you are filing a joint return, figure your energy efficient home improvement credit as follows. 1. Complete lines 17a through 30 of a separate Form 5695 for each main home.'
findings.fix: Word both gates as 'at any home you or your spouse used in 2025', and ask the biomass amounts per main home.

findings.who: A condominium owner or co-op tenant-stockholder whose association or cooperative installed a qualifying biomass boiler for the building in 2025.
findings.why_no: The filer personally installed and paid for nothing at the unit, so answers no to whether anything was installed. Yet the filer is treated as having paid a proportionate share.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 2: 'If you are a member of a condominium management association ... or a tenant-stockholder in a cooperative housing corporation, you are treated as having paid your proportionate share of any costs of such association or corporation.'
findings.fix: Add to the parent gate: 'or did your condo association or housing co-op install such equipment in the building in 2025?' Then ask for the filer's share.

findings.who: A filer who bought and paid for a pellet stove in late 2024, but whose installation was completed in early 2025.
findings.why_no: The filer associates the purchase with 2024 and may answer no to 'installed in 2025', or may have claimed nothing for it in 2024.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 1, Costs: 'costs are treated as being paid when the original installation of the item is completed'
findings.fix: Help text: 'Count it if installation was finished in 2025, even if you paid for it in 2024.'

findings.who: A filer who installed solar panels in 2022 to 2024 and used tax software that showed Form 5695 under 'Forms and Schedules'. Their 2024 tax was too small to use the whole credit, so the 2024 Form 5695 line 16 shows a carryforward.
findings.why_no: Form 5695 attaches to Form 1040 and feeds Schedule 3, line 5a. The filer reads 'Form 1040 or 1040-SR and its schedules' as covering every attachment that flows into the 1040. Or they recall only the 1040 and Schedule 3 and answer no from memory. The gate asks about forms in general, not the credit, so nothing prompts them to recall the solar credit.
findings.irs_text: f5695 (2025) p. 1, line 12: 'Credit carryforward from 2024. Enter the amount, if any, from your 2024 Form 5695, line 16'
findings.fix: Ask about the fact, or add help text naming it: 'Did your (or, on a joint return, your spouse's) 2024 return include Form 5695, Residential Energy Credits, for example for solar, wind, geothermal, battery, or fuel cell property? Count forms attached to your return, such as Form 5695, even if they feed a schedule.' Or ask the line 12 question directly, defaulting to zero when it is blank.

findings.who: A filer whose original 2024 return was Form 1040 alone. In 2025 they filed Form 1040-X adding Form 5695 for 2024 solar property, which left a carryforward on the amended 2024 Form 5695, line 16.
findings.why_no: 'Your 2024 federal income tax return' reads as the return as originally filed, which had no other forms. Nothing says to count an amended return.
findings.irs_text: f5695 (2025) p. 1, line 12: 'Enter the amount, if any, from your 2024 Form 5695, line 16'; i5695 p. 1: 'Also use Form 5695 to take any residential clean energy credit carryforward from 2024'
findings.fix: Add 'as originally filed or as amended (Form 1040-X)' to the gate, or ask directly whether any 2024 Form 5695, original or amended, shows an amount on line 16.

findings.who: A couple married in 2025 who file jointly for 2025. In 2024 the spouse filed a separate single return with Form 5695 and a line 16 carryforward. The filer prepares the return alone and knows only their own 2024 Form 1040.
findings.why_no: The gate does say 'or, on a joint return, your spouse's'. But a filer answering about a return they never saw may answer about their own return only, and the help gives no prompt about a spouse's separate premarital return.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 13: 'A married couple filing jointly report their combined income and deduct their combined allowable expenses on one return'; f5695 line 12
findings.fix: Add help text: 'Include your spouse's 2024 return even if it was filed separately before you married; ask your spouse.'

findings.who: A homeowner whose old central air conditioner failed in summer 2025. The contractor replaced it with a unit that meets the top CEE tier, and the filer chose it for price or availability, not to save energy.
findings.why_no: The parent gate asks whether anything was installed 'to save or make energy'. A replacement for a broken unit was installed to restore cooling, so the filer truthfully answers no about purpose. The central AC question is never reached.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 3, Section B: 'Residential energy property expenditures are costs of new qualified energy property that is installed on or in connection with a home that you used during 2025 ... Qualified energy property is any of the following. • ... central air conditioners'. Qualification depends on the CEE tier, not on why the filer bought it.
findings.fix: Drop the purpose from the parent gate. Ask: 'In 2025, did you or your spouse have any of these installed at a home you used (even as a repair or replacement): insulation, windows, doors, central air conditioner, heat pump, water heater, furnace or boiler, biomass stove, electrical panel or wiring, solar, battery, or other? Or did you pay for a home energy audit?'

findings.who: A tenant-stockholder in a housing cooperative, or a condominium owner. In 2025 the co-op or condo association installed qualifying central air conditioning, and the filer paid for it through assessments or maintenance charges.
findings.why_no: The filer installed nothing personally. The association did the work and the filer paid only assessments, so 'Anything was installed ... at a home' reads as no. Even if the parent were reached, 'A central air conditioner was installed' would not seem to cover the filer's share.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 2, Association or cooperative costs: 'you are treated as having paid your proportionate share of any costs of such association or corporation'
findings.fix: Add to the parent gate: 'or did your condo association or housing co-op install any of these at your building in 2025 (your share counts)?' Carry that yes into the central AC question, and ask for the filer's proportionate share.

findings.who: A filer whose qualifying central air conditioner was installed in 2024 and not claimed then. In 2025 the filer installed a new panelboard to enable it and elects the consecutive-year safe harbor.
findings.why_no: Read with the parent's 'in 2025', the central AC question asks about a 2025 installation. The AC went in during 2024, so the filer answers no, although the safe harbor lets the filer treat it as installed in 2025.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 6, Lines 25a Through 25e, Note: 'If the enabling property and the enabled property were installed in consecutive tax years, then you can treat both as having been installed in the later of the tax year'; Line 25b: 'B - Central air conditioners reported on Form 5695, line 22a'
findings.fix: Ask: 'Was a central air conditioner installed in 2025, or in 2024 together with panel or wiring work done in 2025 to support it?' Then apply the safe-harbor election.

findings.who: A married couple filing jointly who lived apart in separate main homes. The spouse had qualifying central AC installed at the spouse's home, and the filer installed nothing at the filer's own home.
findings.why_no: The gate's wording does not say 'you or your spouse'. A filer reading 'a home' as their own home answers no.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 3, Married taxpayers with more than one home: 'If you are filing a joint return ... Complete lines 17a through 30 of a separate Form 5695 for each main home.'
findings.fix: Word both the parent gate and the child gate as 'you or your spouse ... at any home either of you used in 2025'. Then ask per home.

findings.who: A homeowner who in 2025 replaced only the outdoor condensing unit and coil of a split-system central air conditioner. The new equipment meets the top CEE tier.
findings.why_no: The filer may read 'A central air conditioner was installed' as a whole new system, not a replacement of the main components, and answer no.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 6, Line 22a: 'Enter the QMID and amount you paid for the most expensive central air conditioner that achieves the highest efficiency tier ... established by the Consortium for Energy Efficiency'
findings.fix: Add help: 'Count a new or replacement central (ducted or split-system) air conditioner, including replacing the outdoor unit and coil; the installer can say whether it meets the top CEE tier.'

findings.who: A homeowner replaced a worn or broken front door in 2025 at their main home for security or looks. The new door happens to meet Energy Star requirements and has a QMID.
findings.why_no: The parent gate asks whether anything was installed 'to save or make energy'. Saving energy was not their purpose, so a truthful answer is no, and the doors question is never asked.
findings.line: f5695.line19a_if_doors (and f5695.line19d_i_if_doors, f5695.line19d_ii_if_doors, f5695.line19e_if_doors when more than one door was installed)

findings.fix: Drop the purpose test and ask about the objects: 'In 2025, did you or your spouse install (or have installed) any of these at a home, for any reason: exterior doors, windows or skylights, insulation or air sealing, central air conditioner, water heater, furnace or boiler, heat pump, biomass stove or boiler, electrical panel or circuit work, solar, wind, geothermal, battery or fuel cell? findings.who: A filer who installed new Energy Star exterior doors in 2025 but no solar, heat pump or other equipment.
findings.why_no: They read 'installed ... to save or make energy' as energy equipment such as solar panels, heat pumps or furnaces, not a building part like a door. They answer no without reaching the doors question.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 1: 'A 30% credit, up to a maximum of $1,200, may be allowed for: ... • Exterior doors; • Windows and skylights'
findings.fix: List exterior doors, windows and insulation by name in the parent question or its help, as in the fix above.

findings.who: A condominium owner who is a member of the management association, or a co-op tenant-stockholder. The association or cooperative installed Energy Star exterior doors in 2025 and passed the cost through to owners.
findings.why_no: The filer installed nothing personally and did not pay a door invoice. They read 'Anything was installed ... at a home' as work they arranged at their own unit, so they answer no.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 2: 'If you are a member of a condominium management association for a condominium you own or a tenant-stockholder in a cooperative housing corporation, you are treated as having paid your proportionate share of any costs of such association or corporation.'
findings.fix: Add to the parent gate: 'Include items your condominium association or housing cooperative installed in 2025 if you paid a share of the cost.' Ask the share of door costs on the door lines.

findings.who: A filer whose existing home was reconstructed. The Energy Star exterior doors went in during late 2024, and the filer first used the reconstructed home in 2025.
findings.why_no: The gate says 'installed in 2025'. The doors were physically installed in 2024, so the filer answers no. But reconstruction costs are treated as paid when original use of the reconstructed home begins.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 1: 'costs are treated as being paid when the original installation of the item is completed, or, in the case of costs connected with the reconstruction of your home, when your original use of the reconstructed home begins.'
findings.fix: Add to the parent gate: '...or was installed earlier as part of rebuilding your home and you first lived in the rebuilt home in 2025.'

findings.who: Spouses filing jointly who lived apart in separate main homes. Only the spouse who is not the primary filer installed Energy Star exterior doors at their own main home in 2025.
findings.why_no: The passive 'at a home' does not name the spouse or the spouse's home. The primary filer may think only of their own home and answer no.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 3: 'If you are filing a joint return, figure your energy efficient home improvement credit as follows. 1. Complete lines 17a through 30 of a separate Form 5695 for each main home.'
findings.fix: Say 'at any home you or your spouse lived in during 2025'.

findings.who: A homeowner whose old gas furnace failed in January 2025 and who had it replaced with a high-efficiency gas furnace that meets the CEE top tier. They replaced it because the house had no heat, not to cut energy use.
findings.why_no: The parent asks whether 'Anything was installed in 2025 at a home to save or make energy'. The furnace was installed for heat, not to save or make energy, so a truthful reading of the purpose clause gives no. The child furnace question is then never asked.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 6: 'Line 24a. Enter the QMID and amount you paid for the most expensive natural gas, propane, or oil furnace or hot water boilers that achieve the highest efficiency tier established by the CEE'. The test is the efficiency tier, not why it was installed.
findings.fix: Drop the purpose clause from the parent and list the items: 'In 2025, did you or your spouse install any of these at a home you lived in: a furnace or boiler, water heater, central air conditioner, heat pump, insulation, windows, doors, electrical panel or wiring, biomass stove, solar or battery equipment; or pay for a home energy audit? Answer yes even if it replaced something that broke.'

findings.who: A tenant-stockholder in a housing cooperative, or a condo owner, whose association replaced the building's central gas hot water boiler in 2025 and passed the cost on through an assessment.
findings.why_no: The filer installed nothing and arranged nothing, so they answer no to 'Anything was installed... at a home' or to 'A ... boiler was installed'. They see the assessment as a co-op or HOA charge.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 2, Association or cooperative costs: 'you are treated as having paid your proportionate share of any costs of such association or corporation'
findings.fix: Add to the gate: 'Did your condominium association or housing cooperative install any of these items in 2025 (you are treated as paying your share)?' Then ask for the filer's proportionate share of the cost.

findings.who: A homeowner whose house was rebuilt after a fire. The new qualifying furnace went in during late 2024, and they moved back into the rebuilt home in 2025.
findings.why_no: The parent says 'installed in 2025'. The furnace was physically installed in 2024, so they answer no.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 1, Costs: 'in the case of costs connected with the reconstruction of your home, when your original use of the reconstructed home begins'
findings.fix: Add to the gate: 'or a home of yours was rebuilt and you began living in it again in 2025 (count items installed during the rebuild)'.

findings.who: A married couple filing jointly who lived apart in separate main homes. The spouse installed a qualifying propane furnace at their own home, and the filer answering the questions knows only about their own house.
findings.why_no: 'Anything was installed in 2025 at a home' does not name the spouse or the spouse's separate home. The filer reads it as their own home and answers no.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 3, Married taxpayers with more than one home: 'If you are filing a joint return... Complete lines 17a through 30 of a separate Form 5695 for each main home.'
findings.fix: Say 'at any home you or your spouse lived in during 2025, including a spouse's separate home'. Then ask the gate once for each main home.

findings.who: A filer who installed a qualifying gas furnace or boiler at a second home or vacation home they used in 2025, rather than at their main home.
findings.why_no: Other credits limited to the main home (insulation, windows, audits) lead the filer to read 'a home' as only where they mainly live. They answer no.

findings.fix: Help text: 'Include a second home or vacation home you used in 2025; furnaces and boilers do not have to be in your main home.'

findings.who: A filer who installed a gas combination (combi) boiler that supplies both space heat and domestic hot water.
findings.why_no: They think of it as a 'tankless water heater' and answer no to the furnace or hot water boiler question.

findings.who: A filer who bought a newly built home and first lived in it in 2025. The builder installed a geothermal heat pump in late 2024, before closing.
findings.why_no: The parent question asks whether anything 'was installed in 2025'. The installation finished in 2024, and the filer installed nothing, so they truthfully answer no and the geothermal question is never asked.
findings.irs_text: i5695 (2025) p. 1, Costs: "For purposes of the residential clean energy credit only, costs connected with the construction of a home are treated as being paid when your original use of the constructed home begins"; p. 1, Caution: "The residential clean energy credit (Part I) is available for both existing homes and homes being constructed"
findings.fix: Broaden the parent gate: 'In 2025, did you or your spouse install anything at a home to save or make energy, pay for a home energy audit, or start living in a newly built or rebuilt home (including one that came with solar, geothermal, battery or similar equipment)?' Then ask for the geothermal cost of a new home when its original use began in 2025.

findings.who: A filer whose home was rebuilt after a fire, with a geothermal system put in during the rebuild, finishing in 2024. They moved back in during 2025.
findings.why_no: 'Installed in 2025' is false for them, so they answer no. Yet the costs count as paid when original use of the rebuilt home begins.

findings.who: A condominium owner, or a tenant-stockholder in a housing cooperative. In 2025 the association or co-op installed a shared geothermal heat pump system for the building and charged members a special assessment.

findings.who: A married couple filing jointly who live in different homes for part of 2025. Only the spouse's home got a geothermal heat pump.
findings.why_no: The parent question names no person. A filer answering for themselves thinks of their own home, where nothing was installed, and answers no.
findings.irs_text: i5695 (2025) p. 2: "If you made energy saving improvements to more than one home that you used as a residence during 2025, enter the total of those costs"; p. 2, Joint occupancy: "These rules don't apply to married individuals filing a joint return"

findings.who: A filer whose old furnace and air conditioner failed in 2025. They replaced them with a ground-source (geothermal) heating and cooling system as an ordinary HVAC replacement.

findings.why_no: They read 'Geothermal heat pump property' as the heat pump unit itself, under that name. They did not replace the unit or do not recognize their system's name, so they answer no.

findings.who: A homeowner who replaced insulation in 2025 as part of a repair or remodel whose purpose was not energy savings. Examples: re-insulating an attic after water or fire damage, rigid insulation board installed with a new roof, or insulation added during a kitchen or bath gut renovation or for soundproofing.
findings.why_no: The parent asks whether anything was installed 'to save or make energy'. The filer's purpose was repair, remodeling or noise, so they answer no and never reach the insulation question. Line 18a turns on whether the material is designed to reduce heat loss or gain and meets IECC, not on the filer's motive.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 5, Line 18a: 'Enter the amounts you paid for any insulation material or air sealing material or system ... that is specifically and primarily designed to reduce the heat loss or gain of your home'
findings.fix: Ask about the item, not the motive: 'Was any insulation, air sealing, windows, doors, skylights, heating or cooling equipment, water heater, electrical panel or circuit work installed at your home in 2025 for any reason (including repairs or remodeling), or was a home energy audit paid for?'

findings.who: A filer who in 2025 bought and installed only air-sealing items: caulk, spray foam around penetrations, weatherstripping, a vapor retarder, or house wrap sold to limit infiltration.
findings.why_no: The filer reads 'insulation or air sealing material or systems' as meaning batts, blown-in insulation or a contractor system. They do not count a vapor retarder or weatherstripping, and may also judge such small items not to be 'installed ... to save or make energy' at the parent gate.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 5, Line 18a: 'any insulation material or air sealing material or system (including any vapor retarder or seal to limit infiltration)'
findings.fix: List examples in the child gate's help: 'including caulk, spray foam sealant, weatherstripping, vapor retarders and house wrap, whether you or a contractor installed them.'

findings.who: A filer whose home was being reconstructed: insulation went in during late 2024 work, and the filer first used the reconstructed home in 2025.

findings.who: A homeowner who installed recycled-content cellulose insulation, open-box Energy Star windows, or an unused floor-model exterior door. No one had used any of these items in a home before.

findings.why_no: The parent gate says 'at a home' without naming the spouse. The filer reads it as the home they themselves live in, unlike the gated question, which says 'you (or, on a joint return, your spouse)'.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 2: 'If you made energy saving improvements to more than one home that you used as a residence during 2025, enter the total of those costs'; 'These rules don't apply to married individuals filing a joint return'; Qualified solar water heating property costs: 'The home doesn't have to be your main home.'
findings.fix: Word the parent gate as 'at any home you or your spouse lived in during 2025, including a second or vacation home'.

findings.who: A filer who installed integrated solar thermal roofing, or a hybrid water heater whose energy comes at least half from the sun, and thinks of it as a new roof or a heat-pump water heater.
findings.why_no: The filer does not see the purchase as 'solar water heating property' and answers the child question no.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 2, Qualified solar water heating property costs: 'No costs relating to a solar panel or other property installed as a roof (or portion thereof) will fail to qualify solely because the property constitutes a structural component'; 'if at least half of the energy used by the solar water heating property for such purpose is derived from the sun.'
findings.fix: Add help to the child question: 'Include solar roofing that heats water and any water heater that gets at least half its energy from the sun, even if it also uses electricity or gas.'

findings.who: A filer whose home was being reconstructed. A qualifying high-efficiency gas water heater was physically installed in late 2024, and the filer first moved back in and used the reconstructed home in 2025.
findings.why_no: The parent asks whether anything was 'installed in 2025'. The heater went in during 2024, so a truthful no closes the gate. The instructions instead treat the cost as paid in 2025, when the filer's original use of the reconstructed home began.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 1, Costs: 'costs are treated as being paid when the original installation of the item is completed, or, in the case of costs connected with the reconstruction of your home, when your original use of the reconstructed home begins'
findings.fix: Broaden the parent to: 'In 2025, did you or your spouse finish installing anything at a home to save or make energy, move back into a home that was rebuilt with such items, pay a share of such items through a condo association or co-op, or pay for a home energy audit?'

findings.who: A condominium owner or co-op tenant-stockholder. In 2025 the association or cooperative installed a qualifying central gas water heater in the building and assessed members for it.
findings.why_no: The filer did not install anything and may not regard the building's mechanical room as 'a home'. The parent's wording points to the filer's own improvements, not association costs, so the filer answers no.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 2, Association or cooperative costs: 'you are treated as having paid your proportionate share of any costs of such association or corporation'
findings.fix: Name association and co-op costs in both the parent and the child question, for example: 'including a share you paid through a condominium association or housing cooperative'.

findings.who: A filer whose old gas water heater failed in 2025 and was replaced with a CEE top-tier gas or propane unit, such as a condensing tankless heater, chosen by the plumber.
findings.why_no: The parent asks about things installed 'to save or make energy'. The filer replaced a broken appliance for its own sake and does not see it as an energy improvement, so the filer answers no.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 6, Line 23a: 'Enter the QMID and amounts you paid for the two most expensive natural gas, propane, or oil water heaters that achieve the highest efficiency tier established by the CEE'
findings.fix: Drop the purpose test from the parent. Ask: 'Did you or your spouse have any of these installed in 2025, for any reason, including replacing a broken one: water heater, furnace, boiler, central air conditioner, heat pump, windows, doors, insulation, electrical panel, solar, battery…'. Leave the efficiency test to the child's help.

findings.who: A married couple filing jointly who lived apart in separate main homes. Only the spouse had a qualifying gas water heater installed at the spouse's home.
findings.why_no: If the parent or child is read as asking about 'your home', the filer answers about their own residence only and says no. The instructions require a separate Form 5695 for each main home on a joint return.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 3, Married taxpayers with more than one home: 'If you are filing a joint return, figure your energy efficient home improvement credit as follows. 1. Complete lines 17a through 30 of a separate Form 5695 for each main home.'
findings.fix: Say 'at any home you or your spouse lived in during 2025' in both the parent and the child question.

findings.who: A filer had a new home built with a wind turbine that was finished and installed in 2024. They first moved in and began using the home in 2025.
findings.why_no: The parent gate asks whether anything was "installed in 2025." The turbine was installed in 2024, so a truthful answer is no. Yet the construction rule treats the cost as paid when the filer's original use of the home begins, which was 2025.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 1, Costs: "For purposes of the residential clean energy credit only, costs connected with the construction of a home are treated as being paid when your original use of the constructed home begins"
findings.fix: Broaden the parent gate: "In 2025, was anything installed at a home to save or make energy, did you or your spouse first move into a newly built or rebuilt home that included such equipment, or was a home energy audit paid for?" Then ask the wind question in the same terms.

findings.who: A filer's home was reconstructed after a fire. The turbine was installed in late 2024 as part of the rebuild, and the filer's original use of the rebuilt home began in 2025.
findings.why_no: The installation was completed in 2024, so "installed in 2025" is truthfully no. The reconstruction rule moves the payment date to when original use of the rebuilt home begins.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 1, Costs: "or, in the case of costs connected with the reconstruction of your home, when your original use of the reconstructed home begins"
findings.fix: Add to the gate: "or did you or your spouse begin living in a rebuilt home in 2025 that included energy equipment installed during the rebuild?"

findings.who: A condominium owner or co-op tenant-stockholder whose association or cooperative installed a wind turbine serving the building in 2025, paid from common funds.
findings.why_no: The filer did not install anything at their own unit. They read "installed ... at a home" and "a wind turbine" as their own purchase, so they answer no, even though they are treated as having paid their proportionate share of the cost.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 2, Association or cooperative costs: "you are treated as having paid your proportionate share of any costs of such association or corporation"
findings.fix: Add to the help for both the gate and the wind question: "Include equipment your condominium association or housing cooperative installed. You are treated as paying your share of its cost." Then ask for that share.

findings.who: A rural filer whose wind turbine stands on a separate nearby parcel or field they own, wired to supply their house, rather than on the house or its lot.
findings.why_no: The gate says "installed ... at a home." A turbine standing away from the house reads as not "at" the home, so the filer answers no. The credit instead covers property used "in connection with" the home.
findings.irs_text: i5695 pp. 2-3, Qualified small wind energy property costs: "property that uses a wind turbine to generate electricity for use in connection with your home"
findings.fix: Change "at a home" to "at or for a home (including equipment placed elsewhere that powers the home)."

findings.who: A married couple filing jointly who lived apart in 2025. The spouse installed a wind turbine at the spouse's own separate residence.
findings.why_no: If the filer reads "a home" in the gate as their own home, they answer no. The line 3 question itself includes the spouse, but it is never reached.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 2, Joint occupancy: "These rules don't apply to married individuals filing a joint return"; p. 2, "If you made energy saving improvements to more than one home that you used as a residence during 2025, enter the total of those costs"
findings.fix: Word the parent gate and the wind gate as "at any home you or your spouse lived in during 2025."

findings.who: A filer who installed a residential wind turbine, or a combined solar and wind generator, and does not think of it as "small wind energy property."
findings.why_no: "Small wind energy property" is a legal label. A filer with a sizable or hybrid turbine may decide theirs is not "small" and answer no.
findings.irs_text: i5695 pp. 2-3: "Qualified small wind energy property costs are costs for property that uses a wind turbine to generate electricity"
findings.fix: Ask about the checkable fact: "Was a wind turbine that makes electricity for the home installed (any size, including one combined with solar)?"

findings.who: A homeowner replaced storm-damaged or worn-out exterior windows in their main home in 2025, or added a skylight while remodeling. The new units carry the Energy Star Most Efficient designation. The goal was repair or looks, not saving energy.
findings.why_no: The parent gate asks whether anything was installed "to save or make energy". This filer's honest motive was repair or remodeling, so they truthfully answer no. The credit does not depend on motive, only on whether the item meets the certification requirements.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 6: "Enter the QMID and amounts you paid for the four most expensive exterior windows and skylights that meet Energy Star certification requirements"; p. 3: qualified improvements are building envelope components that "meet certain energy standards". Nothing about purpose.
findings.fix: Drop the purpose from the parent: "In 2025, did you or your spouse have anything installed or replaced at a home you lived in, such as windows, skylights, exterior doors, insulation, a furnace, a water heater, an air conditioner, a heat pump, solar panels or an electrical panel, for any reason, or pay for a home energy audit?" Then test the energy certification at the child question.

findings.who: A condominium owner or cooperative tenant-stockholder whose association replaced the building's exterior windows or skylights in 2025 and charged the owners through a special assessment.
findings.why_no: They did not install anything themselves, and the work was done on the building by the association. So they answer no to "anything was installed ... at a home" and to "exterior windows or skylights were installed". They do not know they count as having paid a proportionate share.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 2: "you are treated as having paid your proportionate share of any costs of such association or corporation"; p. 1, What's New: "a fractional share of the qualified energy efficiency improvements"
findings.fix: Add to the parent gate and its help: "Include work your condominium association or housing cooperative paid for, such as new windows for the building, since you are treated as paying your share." Ask for the filer's share at the window lines.

findings.who: A filer whose existing home was rebuilt after a fire or major damage, with new qualifying windows and skylights. They moved back into the rebuilt home in 2025.
findings.why_no: They think of the project as rebuilding the house, not as installing something to save energy. The 2025 date may also seem not to fit if most of the money was paid in 2024.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 1, Costs: "in the case of costs connected with the reconstruction of your home, when your original use of the reconstructed home begins"
findings.fix: Help for the parent gate: "Count windows and other items in a home that was rebuilt or reconstructed if you began living in the rebuilt home in 2025, even if you paid earlier."

findings.who: A married couple filing jointly who lived apart in separate main homes. New windows were installed only at the spouse's home.
findings.why_no: The filer reads "a home" as their own home and answers about their own house. The gate never says "you or your spouse" or "any home either of you lived in".
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 3: "If both you and your spouse owned and lived apart in separate main homes ... If you are filing a joint return ... Complete lines 17a through 30 of a separate Form 5695 for each main home."
findings.fix: Word the gate as "at any home you or your spouse lived in during 2025". Ask whether the spouses kept separate main homes, and if so, ask the window questions once for each home.
